title: Out-of-Order Execution
summary: How hardware executes instructions as their operands become ready instead of in program order, and Tomasulo's algorithm that makes it possible.

slides.markdown:
In an **in-order** pipeline, instructions issue strictly in program order — if the instruction at the head stalls (say, a cache miss taking 200 cycles), every instruction behind it stalls too, even ones with nothing to do with the miss.

That's a huge waste: a later, fully independent ADD sits idle behind a load it doesn't depend on. **Out-of-order (OoO) execution** exists precisely to let independent instructions bypass a stalled one, extracting the ILP that in-order issue leaves on the table.

**Dynamic scheduling** means the hardware decides *at runtime* which instruction to execute next, based on which operands are actually ready — not the compile-time order the program was written in.

An instruction is issued to execute the moment its inputs are available and a functional unit is free, regardless of instructions ahead of it that are still waiting. This is the core mechanism that turns a stalled load from a whole-pipeline stall into a stall of just that one instruction and its dependents.

**Reservation stations** are small buffers, one per functional unit (or shared among a few), that hold an instruction along with its operands — or placeholders for operands not yet computed — until everything it needs is ready.

An instruction issues into a free reservation station immediately, freeing up the front end to keep fetching, even while the instruction itself waits there for its inputs to arrive. Once all operands show up, the reservation station fires the instruction to its functional unit — decoupling *when an instruction is fetched* from *when it actually executes*.

**Tomasulo's algorithm** (IBM 360/91) is the classic scheme most OoO cores descend from.

![Tomasulo's algorithm's data flow: reservation stations, a common data bus broadcasting results, and register status tracking](assets/tomasulo-dataflow.svg)

Instructions issue into stations tracking ready operands. A result broadcasts on the **CDB** to every waiting station at once — stalled instructions become ready the same cycle.

slides.markdown:
Executing out of order creates a problem: the *outside world* — interrupts, exceptions, register state — must still look like instructions completed **in program order**. The **reorder buffer (ROB)** holds every in-flight instruction's result until it can **commit** in original order, even though execution was out of order.

An instruction can finish long before it commits — it waits in the ROB. This is what makes precise exceptions possible ([exceptions-in-pipelines](exceptions-in-pipelines)): nothing is visible to software until it's that instruction's turn.

| | In-order | Out-of-order |
|---|---|---|
| Issue order | Program order | Data-ready order |
| Hardware needed | Simple | Reservation stations, ROB, wakeup/select logic |
| Achieved ILP | Limited by head-of-line stalls | Much higher — hides latency behind independent work |
| Power/area cost | Low | High — scheduling logic is expensive |

**How to decide:** OoO wins when workloads have unpredictable latencies (cache misses, variable-latency ops) worth hiding; in-order wins where area/power budgets are tight and predictable, in-order-friendly code dominates (many embedded and mobile efficiency cores).
